questions.passage:
Text 1: In an essay on urban trees, author Priya Raman argues that street trees mainly improve a city by slowing traffic: drivers who see leafy canopies tend to reduce speed, she claims, making roads safer for pedestrians.
Text 2: A city transportation report notes that street trees can make drivers feel the road is narrower and less predictable, and some drivers respond by slowing. However, it cautions that trees can also block sightlines at intersections, and the report recommends trimming branches near crosswalks.
questions.q: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
options: It rejects Text 1's claim that street trees affect how drivers behave.
It argues that street trees are more effective at reducing heat than at slowing traffic.
It provides evidence that street trees have no effect on pedestrian safety.
It accepts Text 1's claim that trees can slow drivers but qualifies it by identifying a safety risk that may require management.
questions.explanation: Text 2 agrees that some drivers slow when trees make roads feel narrower and less predictable, supporting Text 1's basic point about speed. It then adds a caution about blocked sightlines and recommends trimming, which qualifies rather than rejects that benefit. The other choices describe claims absent from the report.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: When the community center announced its weekend cooking classes, several residents who had never cooked for a group ______ to sign up, eager to learn inexpensive recipes they could prepare for their families.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: decided
has decided
deciding
decide
questions.explanation: The subject is several residents, which requires a plural past-tense verb to fit the past-tense announcement. Decided supplies the main verb for residents and matches the surrounding tense. Has decided is singular, while decide and deciding do not fit grammatically here.

questions.passage:
A team of ecologists studied three wetland plots to determine whether native grass cover was associated with pollinator visits. They recorded the percentage of native grass cover and the average number of pollinator visits per hour in each plot.
Plot | Native grass cover | Pollinator visits per hour
A | 40% | 12
B | 65% | 21
C | 80% | 25
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship shown by the data?
options: Native grass cover was unrelated to pollinator visits per hour.
Pollinator visits per hour were highest where native grass cover was lowest.
Pollinator visits increased by exactly 10 per hour for every 20% increase in cover.
As native grass cover increased across the plots, pollinator visits per hour also increased.
questions.explanation: The table shows that pollinator visits rise from 12 to 21 to 25 as native grass cover rises from 40% to 65% to 80%, so the two measures increase together across the three plots. The claim of an exact 10-visit gain for every 20% increase does not hold: from 40% to 65% cover, visits rise by 9, and from 65% to 80%, they rise by 4. The other statements contradict the tabled values.

questions.passage: Nadia had rehearsed her presentation for a week, timing each slide and practicing answers to likely questions. Yet as she stood before the scholarship committee, she noticed that the microphone was dead and that the clock behind the judges was fifteen minutes fast. She took a breath, set her notes aside, and ______.
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: spoke directly to the committee without relying on her timed script
concluded that the committee had deliberately sabotaged the microphone
decided to read her notes word for word as planned
asked the committee to postpone the presentation until the equipment was repaired
questions.explanation: Nadia had prepared carefully but encounters equipment problems, and setting her notes aside signals that she adapts rather than freezing or relying on the original script. Speaking directly to the committee fits her controlled response after taking a breath. The other choices either assume hostility, abandon the presentation, or ignore the clear action of setting the notes aside.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Historian Luis Ortega argues that the 1930s construction of a municipal auditorium in a midwestern city strengthened civic life because it gave residents a shared venue for concerts, meetings, and public ceremonies.
Text 2: In a memoir, resident Helen Park recalls attending a concert at the new auditorium but notes that many working-class families could rarely afford tickets, so their participation in the venue's cultural events remained limited. She adds, however, that the building's free public open houses drew large crowds.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Park most likely respond to Ortega's argument?
options: She would agree that the auditorium could foster shared civic experiences but suggest that those benefits were unevenly accessible.
She would claim that the auditorium should not have been built.
She would deny that the auditorium served any civic purpose.
She would argue that the auditorium's concerts were more important than its open houses.
questions.explanation: Park describes free open houses that drew large crowds, which supports Ortega's view that the auditorium could bring residents together. Her point that many working-class families could rarely afford concerts qualifies that civic benefit by showing that access was unequal. She does not deny all civic value or argue that the building should not have been built.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The documentary not only traces the history of the neighborhood's public baths but also ______ how residents fought to preserve them.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: explains
to explain
it explains
explaining
questions.explanation: The not only ... but also structure joins two verbs that share the subject the documentary, so the second part needs the present-tense verb explains. Explaining and to explain are not finite verbs parallel to traces, and it explains repeats the subject unnecessarily.

questions.passage:
A public-health team surveyed 600 adults in a city about whether they walked at least 30 minutes on a typical day. They also recorded whether each respondent lived within a 10-minute walk of a park.
Lives within 10-minute walk of a park | Surveyed | Walked at least 30 minutes
Yes | 360 | 216
No | 240 | 96
questions.q: Which choice best describes the data in the table?
options: The percentage of respondents who reported walking at least 30 minutes was higher among those who lived within a 10-minute walk of a park than among those who did not.
Living near a park caused respondents to walk at least 30 minutes each day.
Among those who lived within a 10-minute walk of a park, fewer than half reported walking at least 30 minutes.
The number of respondents who did not live within a 10-minute walk of a park was greater than the number who did.
questions.explanation: For respondents who lived near a park, 216 out of 360, or 60%, reported walking at least 30 minutes, while 96 out of 240, or 40%, of those who did not live near a park reported doing so. Thus the percentage was higher among the near-park group. The table does not establish causation, and it shows more respondents in the near-park group than in the other group.

questions.passage: At first, the museum's new audio guide seemed like a success: visitors used it at nearly every exhibit. But when staff reviewed the logs, they found that most visitors listened to a stop for only a few seconds before moving on, and several later said they had used the guide mainly to find the nearest restroom. In response, the museum ______.
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: redesigned the guide to feature a smaller number of substantial exhibit descriptions
assumed that visitors were uninterested in the museum's exhibits because they disliked technology
added more restroom locations to every gallery
concluded that visitors should no longer be allowed to use audio guides
questions.explanation: The logs show that visitors were not engaging with long audio stops and often used the guide for practical navigation. A reasonable response would be to make the guide more focused and useful to visitors, as by offering fewer but more substantial descriptions. The other choices are overreactions or unsupported conclusions about technology and the exhibits.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: Many cities plant trees to reduce summer heat. ______, the cooling effect depends on where the trees are placed: a dense canopy over a paved plaza can lower surface temperatures, while isolated trees in a parking lot may provide little relief.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Likewise
However
For example
Therefore
questions.explanation: The first sentence states a general benefit, while the second sentence introduces an important qualification about the effect depending on placement. However signals that contrast or qualification. Therefore and likewise suggest a cause or similarity that the second sentence does not establish, and for example would introduce an illustration rather than a qualification.

questions.passage:
Text 1: A science journalist reports that a team of biologists found that urban foxes in one city avoided areas with artificial lighting, suggesting light pollution reduces their foraging habitat.
Text 2: Another team studying the same city's foxes found that foxes often foraged near lighted train stations late at night, where discarded food was plentiful. The team noted, however, that the foxes usually arrived after the last train, when station lights were dimmed.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would the second team most likely respond to the first team's claim?
options: They would reject it entirely by showing that artificial lighting never affects fox behavior.
They would qualify it by noting that foxes may tolerate some artificial light when food is available, though the timing or intensity of light matters.
They would claim that train stations are the only places where urban foxes find food.
They would argue that food availability matters more than any other factor in every urban habitat.
questions.explanation: The second team observed foxes near train stations only after the last train, when lights were dimmed, which suggests that bright artificial light can still deter them. At the same time, the presence of discarded food shows that some mild or dim lighting may be tolerated when food is available. This qualifies the first team's broad claim rather than rejecting it completely.

questions.passage: During the 1970s, a network of neighborhood libraries in a Midwestern city began lending not only books but also tools, seeds, and kitchen equipment. At first, some officials questioned whether these items fit a library's mission. Over time, however, the lending program brought in residents who had never used the library and increased support for traditional services. Librarians reported that many new patrons later borrowed books and attended literacy classes. The program's director argued that expanding what a library lends can strengthen, rather than dilute, its core educational role.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: New patrons used the library only for tools and kitchen equipment, not for books or classes.
The program's main purpose was to replace traditional library services with nonbook items.
A broader lending program helped a library network attract new patrons and reinforce its educational mission.
Officials quickly agreed that lending tools and seeds was essential to libraries' mission.
questions.explanation: The text explains that lending nontraditional items drew residents who had not used the library and led many of them to borrow books and attend classes, strengthening the library's educational role. The passage says officials initially questioned the program, not that they quickly agreed, and it notes that new patrons later used traditional services, so the claims about exclusive use or replacement are incorrect.

questions.passage: The researchers' conclusion was ______: they had collected data from only one pond and could not rule out local conditions that might have influenced the results. Even the study's authors cautioned that further observations were needed before their findings could be applied more widely.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: ornamental
definitive
uncontroversial
provisional
questions.explanation: The conclusion is based on limited data from a single pond, and the authors themselves say further observations are needed, so it is best described as provisional, or tentative. A definitive conclusion would be treated as final, while ornamental and uncontroversial do not capture the uncertainty described.

questions.passage: Many people assume that coral reefs and the fish that live on them recover at the same rate after a hurricane. In a study of a protected lagoon, researchers found that certain branching corals returned within five years. ______, fish populations that depend on the reef took much longer to recover.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: However
Likewise
Therefore
For example
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the relatively quick return of certain corals with the much slower recovery of fish populations. A contrast transition such as 'However' signals this difference, while cause, example, and similarity transitions misrepresent the relationship.

questions.passage: The temperature dropped sharply overnight______ the crew delayed the roof repairs until the ice melted.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: so
, so
; so
, therefore
questions.explanation: The sentence joins two independent clauses that express a cause-and-effect relationship, so a comma before the coordinating conjunction 'so' is required. Omitting the comma, placing a semicolon before 'so,' or substituting 'therefore' with only a comma creates nonstandard punctuation.

questions.passage: When a local historical society began an oral history project about the town's former railway district, organizers first interviewed only retired rail workers. After listening to the recordings, project lead Nia Brooks noticed that the interviews often focused on machinery and schedules. She then added conversations with teenagers whose families had recently moved to the neighborhood. These interviews described everyday life around the station—the bakeries, bus routes, and gathering spots—details that the older workers had rarely mentioned. Brooks concluded that the project needed multiple generations to capture the district's history fully.
questions.q: According to the text, why did Brooks add interviews with teenagers to the project?
options: To include everyday details about the district that the retired workers had rarely mentioned
To document the technical operation of the railway station
To show that teenagers knew more about railway machinery than older workers did
To replace the retired workers' accounts of machinery and schedules
questions.explanation: The text states that the teenagers described everyday life around the station, including details the older workers had rarely mentioned, and that Brooks wanted multiple generations to capture the history fully. The project did not replace the workers' accounts, which had focused on machinery and schedules, nor did it seek to compare the groups' technical knowledge.

questions.passage: The city expanded its bus service and lowered fares. ______, ridership among students increased by nearly a third within a year.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Nevertheless
As a result
In contrast
Similarly
questions.explanation: Expanding service and lowering fares plausibly caused the rise in student ridership, so a result transition is appropriate. The other transitions would signal contrast or similarity rather than a cause-and-effect relationship.

questions.passage: The mayor's proposal to convert the empty warehouse into a combined library and job-training center was initially described as ______. Some residents worried that the project would increase traffic, while others argued that the site should remain undeveloped. After several public meetings, however, the plan gained widespread support and was approved by the city council.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: lucrative
contentious
mundane
uncontroversial
questions.explanation: The proposal prompted opposing views, with some residents worried about traffic and others wanting the site left undeveloped, so it was contentious, or likely to cause disagreement. The later approval shows that the opposition eased, but it does not make the initial reaction uncontroversial, mundane, or necessarily lucrative.

questions.passage: The curator examined the painting carefully for nearly an hour______ she noticed a faint signature near the frame.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: , therefore,
; therefore
therefore,
; therefore,
questions.explanation: The text contains two independent clauses, so a semicolon can separate them before the conjunctive adverb 'therefore,' which is followed by a comma. A comma before 'therefore' creates a comma splice, and the versions that omit punctuation or the comma after 'therefore' do not follow standard punctuation for joining independent clauses.

questions.passage: In the 1920s, a cooperative of Black farmers in a rural southern county pooled their savings to buy a grain elevator. At the time, private elevator owners set storage fees that many small farmers could not afford, especially after harvest, when prices were low. By storing grain in their own facility and selling later, cooperative members could wait for better prices and share storage costs. The cooperative also negotiated shipping rates as a group. Although the venture faced debt and drought, it lasted for nearly two decades, allowing members to keep more of their earnings and to plan across seasons.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The cooperative was formed mainly to help farmers grow a wider variety of crops.
Private elevator owners lowered their fees after the cooperative was founded.
By pooling resources, a farmers' cooperative gained control over storage and shipping, helping members improve their earnings and manage market pressures.
The cooperative eliminated all financial risk for its members despite drought and debt.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that members pooled money to buy a grain elevator, store grain until prices improved, share costs, and negotiate shipping rates, which helped them keep more earnings. The text says the cooperative still faced debt and drought, does not claim private owners lowered fees, and does not mention crop variety as its purpose.

questions.passage: The historian acknowledged that the mill owners' records offered detailed production figures. ______, she argued that these records were incomplete because they rarely mentioned the workers who supplied the labor.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Nevertheless
Consequently
Similarly
For example
questions.explanation: The second sentence contrasts the records' detailed production figures with the historian's argument that they were incomplete. 'Nevertheless' correctly signals that contrast or concession, while the other transitions would incorrectly suggest a result, similarity, or example.

questions.passage:
• Goal: Write a sentence for a school newsletter explaining how a new bike-share program helped students.
• The program launched in September at Harlow High School.
• By November, 42 percent of students had used a bike at least once.
• The share of students who reported walking or biking to school rose from 18 to 31 percent.
• A local bike shop donated 25 helmets for safety clinics.
• Some students said afternoon wait times for bikes were long.
questions.q: Which choice best accomplishes the student’s goal?
options: After Harlow High launched a bike-share program, the share of students who walked or biked to school rose from 18 to 31 percent, though some students reported long afternoon waits.
A bike-share program lets people borrow bicycles for short trips, usually in exchange for a fee.
Most Harlow High students used the bike-share program at least once by November.
Harlow High’s bike-share program began in September and received 25 donated helmets for safety clinics.
questions.explanation: The correct choice explains how the program helped students by connecting it to the increase in walking and biking, while also acknowledging the noted drawback of afternoon waits. The choice about donated helmets gives a detail but does not explain how the program helped students, and the claim that most students used the program conflicts with the note that 42 percent used it at least once.

questions.passage:
• Goal: Write an introductory sentence for an article arguing that a community garden improved residents’ access to fresh food.
• The garden occupies a vacant lot in the Brookside neighborhood.
• In its first year, 60 families rented plots for $20 each.
• A nearby grocery closed two years earlier.
• A survey found that 70 percent of gardeners ate more vegetables than before joining.
questions.q: Which choice best accomplishes the student’s goal?
options: After a nearby grocery closed, a new community garden in Brookside gave 60 families a place to grow fresh food; most gardeners later reported eating more vegetables.
Community gardens across the country are popular, but they often require volunteers to build raised beds.
The Brookside community garden charges $20 per plot and includes a shed and three raised beds.
Because the Brookside garden has 60 plots, the neighborhood should open a second garden.
questions.explanation: The correct choice introduces the article’s argument by linking the garden to increased access to fresh food and to the survey finding about eating more vegetables. The choice about plot fees and raised beds supplies minor details, while the recommendation to open a second garden does not introduce the argument about improved food access.

questions.passage:
• Goal: Write a sentence for a history presentation emphasizing the economic effects of a 1912 mill strike in the fictional town of Calder.
• Mill owners hired replacement workers during the strike.
• Local shops reported sales fell nearly 30 percent.
• The strike lasted six weeks.
• Workers demanded shorter hours and safer machinery.
• After the strike, the mill installed guards on two machines.
questions.q: Which choice best accomplishes the student’s goal?
options: During the six-week strike, the mill owners’ hiring of replacement workers contributed to a nearly 30 percent drop in sales at local shops.
In 1912, a strike in Calder divided the town and lasted six weeks.
Workers in Calder struck for six weeks to demand shorter hours and safer machinery.
After the strike, the mill installed guards on two machines.
questions.explanation: The correct choice focuses on an economic effect of the strike by connecting the hiring of replacement workers to the sharp decline in local shop sales. The choice about workers’ demands explains why the strike happened, and the choice about machine guards describes a later safety change rather than the economic impact of the strike.

questions.passage: A student claims that extending a public library’s weekday hours to 8 p.m. has increased teenagers’ use of the library. The Harlow Public Library made the change in January.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the student’s claim?
options: A survey found that many teenagers prefer to study at home because it is quieter.
Weekend visits by adults increased by 10 percent after the library added a new reading area.
The library added more young adult novels in January, and teen checkouts of those novels increased.
Between January and May, visits by teenagers from 6 to 8 p.m. rose by about 45 percent, while teen visits earlier in the day stayed roughly the same.
questions.explanation: The correct finding directly supports the claim because it shows increased use by teenagers specifically during the newly extended evening hours, while teen visits at other times did not rise similarly. The finding about young adult novels suggests another possible reason for increased teen use, so it does not isolate the effect of extended hours.

questions.passage: A team of biologists studying a desert ant found that foragers could return to the nest in a straight line even when the sun was briefly hidden by a screen. The team hypothesized that the ants use the sky’s polarization pattern, rather than landmarks, for navigation.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team’s hypothesis?
options: Ants returned to the nest quickly whenever the researchers placed food near familiar landmarks.
Ants sometimes paused in the shade during the hottest part of the day.
When researchers altered the polarization pattern while leaving landmarks unchanged, the ants’ return paths became more winding.
Ants were more likely to forage when the temperature was below 40°C.
questions.explanation: The correct finding supports the hypothesis because changing the polarization pattern alone disrupted the ants’ navigation even though landmarks stayed the same. The choice about food near familiar landmarks points toward landmark use and does not support reliance on polarization, while the other choices describe behavior unrelated to navigation cues.

questions.passage: Ecologist Priya Rao argues that the decline of the silver warbler in the Redstone Reserve is caused mainly by nest parasitism by cowbirds, not by a shortage of insects.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly strengthen Rao’s argument?
options: Warbler numbers fell more sharply in areas where insect abundance was lower during nesting season.
Cowbirds were often seen near warbler nests in the reserve.
Some warblers built nests in shrubs rather than in trees.
In areas of the reserve where cowbird traps reduced parasitism, warbler nesting success increased even though insect abundance did not change.
questions.explanation: The correct finding strengthens Rao’s argument by showing that reducing cowbird parasitism improved warbler nesting success even when insect abundance stayed the same, which points to parasitism rather than insects as the main cause. The finding about lower insect abundance and sharper declines would support the competing explanation, and merely seeing cowbirds near nests does not establish their effect on warbler numbers.

questions.passage: In the opening of her essay, historian Elena Ruiz describes a crowded 1890s train platform. She then turns to the account books of a small family-owned hotel near the station, using room rates and guest logs to show how the town’s economy changed after rail service arrived. Ruiz closes by comparing that town with two others that never received a station.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of Ruiz’s essay?
options: It defines a key term and gives examples of its everyday use.
It states a thesis and then refutes opposing views with statistics.
It presents a vivid scene, then analyzes financial records to trace an economic change, and ends with a comparison.
It tells a chronological story from the perspective of a single hotel guest.
questions.explanation: The correct choice follows the passage’s sequence: a descriptive opening scene, an analysis of hotel account books to explain economic change, and a closing comparison with towns that lacked a station. The other choices misidentify the essay’s movement, such as treating it as a refutation of opposing views or as a single guest’s chronological story.

questions.passage: Popular accounts often present scientific discovery as a sudden flash of insight from a single researcher. Yet a closer look at the development of a new type of water filter in a small public laboratory shows a different pattern: chemists, city engineers, and residents tested dozens of prototypes over two years, with each failure reshaping the next design. The writer describes this process not to minimize individual creativity but to show how shared testing can turn a promising idea into a reliable tool.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To challenge the lone-genius view by illustrating how collaboration and repeated testing contributed to a practical invention
To describe the chemical composition of a new water filter in detail
To explain why residents should distrust city engineers
To argue that individual creativity is irrelevant to scientific progress
questions.explanation: The correct choice captures the text’s central aim: it contrasts the popular lone-genius image with a collaborative process of repeated testing that produced a reliable water filter. The text explicitly says it does not aim to minimize individual creativity, and it gives no detailed chemical composition or warning about city engineers.

questions.passage:
Text 1: A city council member argues that converting a vacant lot into a pocket park will reduce summer heat because the pavement will be replaced by grass and trees. She cites neighborhood temperature readings showing that the lot is hotter than surrounding blocks.

Text 2: A parks department report notes that pocket parks can reduce heat, but only if trees mature and are watered during drought. It warns that newly planted grass can die in dry summers without steady maintenance, leaving bare soil that absorbs heat.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
options: Text 1 presents temperature data, while Text 2 rejects the idea that trees affect temperature.
Text 1 emphasizes a benefit of replacing the vacant lot with a pocket park, while Text 2 qualifies that benefit by noting that it depends on maintenance.
Text 2 argues that vacant lots are generally cooler than pocket parks.
Both texts agree that pocket parks always reduce heat regardless of upkeep.
questions.explanation: The correct choice accurately contrasts the texts: the first presents a park as a way to reduce heat, and the second accepts that possibility while stressing conditions such as mature trees and watering. The other choices misrepresent the texts by making them agree without qualification, by claiming that Text 2 rejects trees’ effect on temperature, or by reversing the comparison between lots and parks.

questions.passage:
Text 1: In a museum planning memo, curator Ana Torres argues that digital replicas of fragile artifacts can broaden access: visitors who cannot travel to the museum can view detailed 3-D models online, and original objects can be preserved in climate-controlled storage.

Text 2: In a response, historian Marcus Bell agrees that digital replicas are useful, but he contends that a museum visit should still include original objects whenever possible. Replicas, he writes, can make artifacts look weightless or interchangeable, while physical objects give visitors a sense of scale and material history.
questions.q: Which choice best describes a difference in emphasis between the two texts?
options: Both texts argue that climate-controlled storage is the main purpose of museums.
Text 1 emphasizes the access and preservation benefits of digital replicas, while Text 2 emphasizes the value of original objects for visitors’ experience.
Text 1 argues that replicas should replace all original displays, while Text 2 says museums should stop using replicas.
Text 2 argues that digital replicas are too expensive to produce.
questions.explanation: The correct choice identifies the main contrast: the curator stresses how replicas expand access and protect fragile originals, while the historian stresses what original objects add to a visitor’s experience. Text 1 does not say all originals should be replaced, Text 2 does not reject replicas entirely, and neither text discusses production costs as the main concern.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: At last year's science fair, Priya and her lab partner ______ their poster on water filtration to a panel of judges.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: have presented
presents
present
presented
questions.explanation: The sentence refers to a completed event last year, and the compound subject “Priya and her lab partner” takes the plural past-tense verb “presented.” “Presents” is singular present tense, and “have presented” does not fit the definite past-time context of last year's fair.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The company will open a new headquarters downtown next year. ______, it will renovate its current offices for use by its research division.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: In contrast
Therefore
For example
In addition
questions.explanation: The second sentence adds another plan to the first plan, so the additive transition “In addition” is appropriate. “Therefore” would incorrectly suggest a cause-and-effect relationship, while “For example” and “In contrast” do not match the relationship between two separate company plans.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The collection of sketches that Ms. Barrett found in her grandmother's attic ______ donated to the local historical society last spring.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: were
have been
was
are
questions.explanation: The subject is “The collection,” which is singular, so the singular past-tense verb “was” agrees with it and fits the past-time phrase “last spring.” The plural forms “were” and “have been” incorrectly agree with “sketches,” which is not the subject of the main clause.

questions.passage:
A school counselor compared the mean number of minutes students spent on homework each week in three afterschool programs.
Program | Students | Mean weekly homework minutes
Robotics | 40 | 120
Drama | 30 | 95
Debate | 50 | 150
questions.q: Which choice best describes the data in the table?
options: Debate participants had the highest mean number of weekly homework minutes.
Robotics participants had exactly twice the mean number of weekly homework minutes of Debate participants.
Drama participants had a higher mean number of weekly homework minutes than Robotics participants.
Drama participants had the highest mean number of weekly homework minutes.
questions.explanation: The table shows Debate with a mean of 150 minutes per week, the largest value among the three programs. Robotics is second at 120 minutes, and Drama has the lowest value at 95 minutes, so the claims that Drama is highest or above Robotics are incorrect. Robotics is not exactly twice the Debate value: twice 150 is 300, not 120.

questions.passage:
A community group tested soil at three neighborhood gardens for lead. Members collected the following samples and recorded how many had lead concentrations above 40 parts per million (ppm). The group wants to identify the site with the greatest percentage, not the greatest number, of samples above 40 ppm.
Site | Samples | Samples above 40 ppm
Ash | 50 | 18
Birch | 40 | 8
Cedar | 80 | 24
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to answer the question?
options: Cedar, where 24 samples were above 40 ppm.
Ash, where 36% of samples were above 40 ppm.
Cedar, where 30% of samples were above 40 ppm.
Birch, where 20% of samples were above 40 ppm.
questions.explanation: The percentages are Ash 18 ÷ 50 = 36%, Birch 8 ÷ 40 = 20%, and Cedar 24 ÷ 80 = 30%. Ash has the greatest percentage above 40 ppm, even though Cedar has the largest raw count of such samples. The question asks for the greatest percentage, so the raw count for Cedar is not the correct basis for the answer.

questions.passage: During the 1910s, many rural communities in the region did not have a high school within walking distance. Some families sent their teenagers to board in nearby towns during the week so the students could attend school. Because this arrangement required payment for room and board, ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: students who boarded rarely attended classes.
access to high school often depended on a family's financial resources.
nearby towns built new high schools only for boarders.
most rural families preferred boarding to walking.
questions.explanation: The text explains that attending high school away from home required families to pay for room and board, which supports the inference that financial resources shaped access. The other choices introduce claims about preferences, school construction, or attendance that the text does not support.

questions.passage:
Text 1: A local historian notes that after Riverbend opened a trolley line in 1912, downtown storefront vacancies fell sharply. The historian concludes that the trolley line caused more shoppers from outlying neighborhoods to visit downtown.
Text 2: Another researcher observes that Riverbend also began a major street-paving project the same year, making travel by wagon and automobile easier. This researcher cautions against attributing downtown recovery to any single change.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would the researcher in Text 2 most likely respond to the historian's conclusion?
options: By claiming that trolley lines have no effect on where shoppers travel.
By asserting that street paving was completed before the trolley line opened.
By arguing that storefront vacancies are not useful evidence about downtown activity.
By suggesting that another simultaneous change may have contributed to the downtown recovery.
questions.explanation: Text 2 points to street paving in the same year and warns against crediting downtown recovery to one change, so the researcher would emphasize a possible additional cause. The text does not deny all effects of trolleys, reject vacancy data entirely, or claim that paving came before the trolley line.

questions.passage: At first, the town's seed library seemed modest: a few labeled envelopes in wooden drawers at the public library. Within two years, volunteers had cataloged hundreds of locally adapted varieties, and gardeners were returning seeds from successful plants. The library now holds workshops on saving seeds and keeps notes on which varieties grow well in the region's sandy soil. What began as a borrowing service has become a shared archive of local growing knowledge.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Gardeners in the region prefer sandy soil to other kinds of soil.
A small seed-lending project grew into a resource for preserving and sharing local growing knowledge.
Seed libraries should lend only varieties that grow well locally.
The public library's wooden drawers are too small for the seed collection.
questions.explanation: The passage traces the seed library from a modest set of envelopes to a larger archive with workshops and local growing records, so the main idea is its growth into a shared knowledge resource. The other choices focus on minor details or make recommendations not given in the text.

questions.passage: In a study of urban birds, researchers placed feeders at half of 40 small parks and left the other half without feeders. Over two seasons, they recorded the number of bird species observed in each park. Parks with feeders attracted more birds, but the increase was concentrated among a few common species; the number of rare species did not rise. The researchers concluded that feeding stations can change where birds gather without necessarily increasing local species diversity.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Bird feeders should be removed from urban parks to protect rare birds.
Bird feeders can increase the number of birds in parks without increasing the variety of species.
Rare bird species were more likely to gather at parks with feeders.
Parks without feeders lost common bird species over two seasons.
questions.explanation: The passage reports that feeders attracted more birds, mostly common species, while rare species did not increase, supporting the idea that feeders can affect bird numbers without increasing species diversity. The other choices contradict the findings or introduce a recommendation the researchers did not make.

questions.passage: At a coastal archaeological site, a team of materials scientists studied concrete blocks made roughly two thousand years ago. They found that small lumps of lime in the concrete sometimes helped it repair itself. When seawater entered a crack, it dissolved material from the lime lump, and new minerals formed that filled the gap. The team emphasizes that the effect depended on the concrete's particular mixture and repeated contact with seawater. Modern concrete containing lime would not necessarily become self-repairing in the same way.
questions.q: According to the text, what role can the lime lumps play in the ancient concrete?
options: They make any modern concrete containing lime self-repairing.
They weaken the concrete by allowing cracks to grow wider.
They prevent seawater from entering cracks in the concrete.
They can help fill cracks when seawater dissolves material from them and new minerals form.
questions.explanation: The text states that seawater dissolves material from a lime lump and that new minerals then fill the crack, so the lime lumps can contribute to self-repair. The passage specifically says modern concrete with lime would not necessarily become self-repairing, and it does not say the lumps block seawater or widen cracks.

questions.passage: While restoring a historic theater, conservators found that the original paint contained lead. They replaced the affected layers with safer materials. ______, they preserved several small samples behind a protective panel so future researchers could study the original pigments.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Instead
For example
In addition
Nevertheless
questions.explanation: The sentence about preserving samples describes an additional action taken alongside the replacement of the paint, so 'In addition' marks the additive relationship. 'Nevertheless' would signal contrast, 'For example' would introduce an illustration, and 'Instead' would suggest a replacement rather than an additional step.

questions.passage: Some city planners warn that protected bike lanes can slow car traffic and hurt nearby businesses. A five-year study of 14 commercial corridors in a mid-sized city, however, found that sales at stores beside the new lanes rose slightly after installation. The increase was modest, and the study could not prove causation. ______, the findings suggest that fears about immediate economic harm may be overstated.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: In other words
For instance
As a result
Even so
questions.explanation: The sentence concedes that the sales increase was modest and not proven causal, but it still draws a cautious conclusion that fears may be overstated. 'Even so' correctly signals that contrast and concession. 'As a result' falsely makes the conclusion an effect of the caveat, while 'For instance' and 'In other words' do not fit the shift in reasoning.

questions.passage: Many people assume that moths are uniformly drab insects with brown or gray wings. ______, the moonwing moth has wings that shimmer with pale yellow and pink scales.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Likewise
Therefore
However
For example
questions.explanation: The second sentence presents a colorful moth that contrasts with the assumption of uniformly drab wings, so a contrast transition is needed. 'However' marks that contrast. 'Therefore' suggests causation, 'For example' would incorrectly treat the colorful moth as an example of drabness, and 'Likewise' would suggest similarity.

questions.passage: When the laboratory's yearlong trial produced disappointing results, the scientist was praised for her ______ account of the failed experiment: she described every error without trying to excuse it.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: tentative
candid
ornate
guarded
questions.explanation: The colon explains that the scientist described every error without excusing it, so the account was frank and honest. 'Candid' conveys that openness. 'Guarded' is the opposite, 'ornate' describes an elaborate style, and 'tentative' suggests uncertainty rather than honesty.

questions.passage: The review was not ______: it examined every study in the field, compared their methods in detail, and explained why their conclusions sometimes conflicted.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: lucid
scathing
tentative
cursory
questions.explanation: The colon lists evidence that the review was thorough, so the blank must mean the opposite of superficial or hasty. 'Cursory' means quick and superficial, and the phrase 'not cursory' fits that logic. 'Scathing' means harshly critical, 'lucid' means clear, and 'tentative' means uncertain; none is directly contradicted by the evidence of detailed examination.

questions.passage: Because the museum's roof had leaked for years ______ moved the most fragile textiles to a climate-controlled storage room before the storm arrived.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: ; staff
: staff
, staff
and staff
questions.explanation: The opening dependent clause beginning with 'Because' must be separated from the main clause by a comma, producing 'years, staff moved.' A semicolon or colon cannot separate a dependent clause from its main clause, and 'and staff' would not repair the missing main-clause structure.

questions.passage: In her new collection of essays, the novelist, who had lived in the region for decades ______ about its shifting seasons with unusual precision, noting both their beauty and their unpredictability.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: — wrote
and wrote
; wrote
, wrote
questions.explanation: The relative clause beginning with 'who had lived' is nonessential and already opened by a comma after 'novelist,' so it must be closed by a comma before the main verb 'wrote.' A semicolon or a single dash would not correctly close this nonrestrictive element, and adding 'and' would make 'wrote' part of the relative clause, leaving the sentence without a main verb.

questions.passage:
• Student's goal: Write a sentence for a science club flyer that explains why the club is launching a campus seed library.
• The environmental science club wants to encourage students to grow some of their own food.
• The seed library will let students borrow seeds for free and return seeds after harvest.
• It will include seeds for drought-tolerant herbs suited to the region.
• A local garden center donated $600 for shelving.
questions.q: Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: The environmental science club is launching a seed library because a local garden center donated $600 for shelving.
The environmental science club will use a $600 donation from a local garden center to buy shelving for a seed library that includes drought-tolerant herbs.
By offering free seeds that students can borrow and later return after harvest, the environmental science club hopes to encourage students to grow some of their own food.
Students who want to grow drought-tolerant herbs should borrow seeds for free and return them after harvest to the local garden center.
questions.explanation: The goal is to explain why the club is starting the seed library. The correct sentence states the club's purpose, encouraging students to grow their own food, and briefly explains the free borrow-and-return system that supports that purpose. The other choices emphasize donations, shelving, or herb varieties without giving the club's reason, and one incorrectly says seeds are returned to the garden center.

questions.passage:
• Student's goal: Write a sentence for a community newsletter that emphasizes both how a planned mural will be created and one benefit it is expected to provide.
• Local students will design the mural for a wall near the farmers market.
• Residents suggested images of neighborhood gardens and local history.
• Students will spend six weeks planning and painting the mural with guidance from a professional artist.
• Similar murals in nearby towns have drawn visitors and discouraged graffiti.
questions.q: Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: Residents suggested images for a mural that a professional artist will paint near the farmers market, which may attract visitors.
Because similar murals in nearby towns have drawn visitors and discouraged graffiti, local students should design a mural near the farmers market.
Local students will design a mural near the farmers market that includes images of neighborhood gardens and local history suggested by residents.

After residents suggested images of neighborhood gardens and local history, local students will spend six weeks planning and painting a mural near the farmers market, which is expected to draw visitors and discourage graffiti, as similar murals have in nearby towns.
questions.explanation: The correct option covers both parts of the goal: it describes students planning and painting the mural over six weeks after resident input, and it states a likely benefit, drawing visitors and discouraging graffiti. The other choices either omit the benefit or misrepresent who will create the mural.

questions.passage:
• Student's goal: Write a sentence for a library newsletter that explains why the town should start a bilingual volunteer program at the public library.
• A town survey found that 18 percent of residents speak a language other than English at home.
• Bilingual volunteers could help patrons complete forms and locate materials.
• The library already offers English conversation classes twice a week.
• A similar program in a neighboring town served 140 families in its first six months.
• Starting the program would cost $1,800 for training and materials.
questions.q: Which choice best accomplishes the student's goal?
options: The library's English conversation classes meet twice a week and could be expanded with $1,800 for training and materials.

Because a town survey found that 18 percent of residents speak a language other than English at home, bilingual volunteers could help patrons complete forms and find materials, much as a similar program in a neighboring town served 140 families in its first six months.
A neighboring town's bilingual volunteer program served 140 families in six months, while the town's library offers English conversation classes twice a week.
Residents who speak a language other than English at home should attend English conversation classes twice a week.
questions.explanation: The goal is to explain why the town should start a bilingual volunteer program. The correct sentence combines the local need, 18 percent of residents speaking a language other than English at home, with what volunteers would do and evidence that a similar program has served families. The other choices focus on existing classes, unrelated comparisons, or a recommendation that residents attend classes rather than explaining the proposed volunteer program.

questions.passage: A team of ecologists studying a suburban prairie argues that seeding native wildflowers along the edges of restored grasslands supports native bees more effectively than mowing alone does. In a two-year study, the team compared plots that were mowed regularly with plots that were mowed and then seeded with a mix of native wildflowers. The team recorded the number of native bee species and the frequency of bee visits to flowers in each plot.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's claim?
options: Mowing alone reduced the cover of nonnative grasses more than seeding wildflowers did.
The seeded plots had a greater variety of native bee species and more frequent bee visits than the mowed-only plots in both years.
Native bee species in the region were more sensitive to temperature than to the availability of flowers.
Both types of plots attracted the same number of native bee species, but the seeded plots had more flowering plants.
questions.explanation: The claim concerns whether seeding wildflowers supports native bees better than mowing alone. A finding that seeded plots had both greater native bee species variety and more frequent bee visits directly shows that benefit. The option about nonnative grasses addresses plants rather than bees, and the temperature finding does not compare the two treatments' effects on bees.

questions.passage: An essay by a historian examines how public libraries in the early twentieth century expanded beyond book lending to include children's reading rooms, lecture halls, and evening classes. The essay then notes that many libraries today are adding tool-lending programs and recording studios. The historian concludes that libraries' lasting strength has been their ability to adapt their services to local needs while preserving free access to knowledge.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Early twentieth-century libraries offered more services than today's libraries do.
Tool-lending programs and recording studios have replaced book lending in many libraries.
Children's reading rooms were the most important innovation in library history.
Public libraries have endured partly by adapting their services while maintaining free access to knowledge.
questions.explanation: The text traces examples of libraries changing their services over time and ends by identifying adaptability along with free access as their enduring strength. The other options either overstate a single detail or make a claim that the passage does not support.

questions.passage:
Text 1: A city council member argues that downtowns must convert empty offices into apartments. She notes that office occupancy has remained below half of pre-pandemic levels in some districts, leaving nearby cafes and shops without customers. Housing downtown, she claims, would create steady foot traffic and make better use of buildings that no longer attract office tenants.

Text 2: An urban economist cautions that office-to-housing conversions are costly and often impractical because many buildings have deep floor plans and outdated plumbing. He adds that cities can encourage housing near downtowns through zoning reforms and transit investment, which would help both residents and businesses without depending on conversions alone.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
options: Text 2 argues that empty offices should remain vacant because housing is too costly to build.
Text 2 dismisses the problem described in Text 1 as unimportant to downtown businesses.
Text 2 shares Text 1's concern about downtowns but presents office conversion as a limited option and favors broader housing policies.
Text 2 agrees that office conversion is the only practical way to bring residents downtown.
questions.explanation: Text 1 proposes office conversion as a response to vacant downtown offices. Text 2 does not reject the downtown problem, but it stresses conversion difficulties and recommends zoning and transit measures as broader alternatives, so it treats conversion as limited rather than sufficient.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The director of the new community center wanted the building to reflect the neighborhood's history. Each of the murals in the center's main hallway ______ a story about the neighborhood's immigrant families.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: have told
tells
are telling
tell
questions.explanation: The subject is Each of the murals, which is singular, so it requires the singular verb tells. The plural forms tell, are telling, and have told do not agree with the singular subject.
